summary: Specifies particular octet sequences that make up the OSI upper-layer protocols (Session, Presentation and ACSE) when used by applications with basic communication needs. It is a practical reference for implementers and is informational.

eli5.summary: A cheat sheet showing the exact bytes an old kind of network software must send to say hello and start talking.

questions: how to implement osi session presentation acse
subtitle: The exact byte sequences for basic OSI communications over Session, Presentation, and ACSE.

tldr.problem: OSI's upper-layer protocols (Session, Presentation, and ACSE) are complex and have many options, but most applications need only a basic subset for simple connection-oriented communication.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents the exact octet sequences (byte sequences) that comprise these protocols when used for basic communications: connection setup, data transfer, and graceful or abrupt shutdown.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can build OSI stacks without reading the full standards, knowing they can interwork with standards-based implementations for basic applications, though they may not claim full conformance.

today: RFC 1698 remains an informational reference for implementers of OSI upper-layer protocols targeting basic communication applications. It is not an Internet Standard and has never been obsoleted. It sits alongside the full ISO standards, offering a practical shortcut for developers who need interworking without full conformance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The OSI upper-layer protocols (Session, Presentation, and ACSE) are large and flexible, with many options. However, most applications need only a basic subset: the ability to create a connection, exchange data, and close the connection. This RFC sidesteps reading the full International Standards by documenting the exact octet sequences (the raw bytes on the wire) needed to support these basic communication requirements.

Instead of implementing every feature of the standards, developers can send these specific byte sequences and interpret received variations, allowing interworking with standards-based implementations. The key insight is that you do not need to implement the full abstract layer structure of OSI; the octet sequences are all that matters.
sections.eli5: Instead of learning all the rules of grammar to write a letter, you just copy the exact format and words that work every time.

sections.title: Abstract and Transfer Syntax
sections.content:
OSI distinguishes between abstract syntax (the meaning of data) and transfer syntax (how it is encoded on the wire). The Presentation layer negotiates which transfer syntax to use for a given abstract syntax. For example, application data might be described in ASN.1 (abstract syntax) and sent using Basic Encoding Rules or BER (transfer syntax).

For migrant protocols (non-OSI protocols running over OSI), a generic anonymous name can be used. For ASN.1-defined abstract syntaxes, specific object identifiers must be used. Presentation context negotiation happens on connection setup: the initiator offers a list of syntaxes, and the responder picks one and confirms it in the reply.
sections.eli5: Imagine your friend speaks English but knows French too. At the start of a conversation, you both decide: are we talking English or French? Once you pick, you stick with it.

sections.title: Messages and Protocol Data Units
sections.content:
A complete connection follows a sequence of messages. To create a connection, the initiator sends a Session CONNECT carrying a Presentation CONNECT carrying an ACSE A-ASSOCIATE request, optionally with application data. The responder replies with Session ACCEPT carrying Presentation CONNECT response carrying ACSE response (AARE).

During the data phase, the sender uses Session S-DATA with Presentation P-DATA carrying the application data. To close gracefully, one side sends Session FINISH with a Presentation and ACSE RELEASE request, and the other side replies with Session DISCONNECT and RELEASE response. To abort, either side can send Session ABORT with no other data, or abruptly disconnect the transport. The RFC shows the exact octet sequences for all these messages, including optional application data, connection rejection, and abort accept.
sections.eli5: Like a phone call: you dial (CONNECT), both say hello (ASSOCIATE), you chat (S-DATA), then one says goodbye (RELEASE) and the other says goodbye back (DISCONNECT), or someone just hangs up (ABORT).

sections.title: Encoding and Length Fields
sections.content:
Both Session and ASN.1/BER use type-length-value encoding, but differently. Session uses a single length octet for lengths under 255, or 0xFF followed by two big-endian octets for larger lengths. ASN.1/BER offers more flexibility: lengths can be short (one octet for values under 127), long (high bit set, followed by the length in a variable number of octets), or indefinite (0x80, then data, then two zero octets).

To interwork, implementations must accept any of these forms when receiving. The RFC recommends sending indefinite length for all constructed BER items (except a few exceptions). This means the length of varying fields like user data affects only that item's length, not the enclosing lengths, making templates easier to use.
sections.eli5: It's like writing a package label: you can write the size in short form if it fits, or use extra digits. Others reading the label must understand both ways.

sections.title: Octet Sequences for Connection, Data, and Close
sections.content:
The RFC then gives nine sections of detailed hex sequences: connection request (6.1), successful reply (6.2), rejection (6.3), data-phase message (6.4), release request (6.5), release response (6.6), deliberate abort (6.7), provider abort (6.8), and abort accept (6.9). Each is presented as a column of tag, length, and value, with comments explaining what each field is.

For example, the connection request includes a CONNECT SPDU (Session Protocol Data Unit), Protocol Options, Session User Requirements (functional units), an optional Called Session Selector, and User Data containing the Presentation CONNECT with ACSE A-ASSOCIATE request. The ACSE section defines application context, called and calling AP-titles and AE-qualifiers, and optional user information carrying the application protocol data.
sections.eli5: Like a blueprint showing how to assemble a bookshelf: each step shows you what piece to add, how big it is, and what it connects to.

viz.caption: Connection States in OSI Basic Communication

items.title: Connection Establishment
items.text: Initiator sends CONNECT with ASSOCIATE request; responder accepts or rejects.

items.title: Data Transfer
items.text: Both sides send S-DATA with application data using negotiated presentation context.

items.title: Graceful Release
items.text: One side sends FINISH with RELEASE request; other replies with DISCONNECT and response.

items.title: Abrupt Abort
items.text: Either side sends ABORT, or simply closes the transport connection.
